```{r options, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>", fig.width = 7,
                      fig.height = 4.5, fig.align = "center", dpi = 96)
old_options <- options(digits = 3, width = 90)
```

A sentence encoder reads a bounded window of text. Every model in `sbert`
has a maximum input length, counted in the sub-word tokens of its
tokenizer, and anything beyond it is cut off before the model sees it. For
the default `all-MiniLM-L6-v2` the window is 256 tokens. Short texts such as
feedback messages, survey answers or titles fit within it. Research abstracts,
open-ended essays and reports do not: the embedding of a long document then
describes its opening only, and whatever the document says after the cut
plays no part in its topic.

A second problem remains even when a document fits. A topic model assigns
each modeled unit to one topic, so a document that discusses two things,
for example a study design and a policy recommendation, is forced into one
of them. Splitting documents into sentences or clauses addresses both
problems: every unit fits the window, and a document takes part in as many
topics as its parts do. This guide shows how `segment()` splits text, how
its options control the length and quality of the units, and how a
segmented topic model reports results per segment and per document.

```{r setup}
library(sbert)
```

## Data

`covid` holds `r format(nrow(covid), big.mark = ",")` abstracts of
educational research published during the COVID-19 pandemic.

- **`Abstract`:** the text that is segmented. Some records carry the
  placeholder `"[No abstract available]"` and are removed first.
- **`Year`:** year of publication. Not used here.

The topic models in this guide need sentence embeddings, which are not
bundled for these abstracts. Segmentation itself needs no model, so every
segmentation below runs on the real abstracts; the segmented topic models
are shown on a small toy example with hand-written embeddings, and the
corresponding code for the abstracts is shown but not run.

```{r data}
abstracts <- subset(covid, Abstract != "[No abstract available]")
nrow(abstracts)
```

`r format(nrow(abstracts), big.mark = ",")` abstracts remain. A word count
is the measure of length used throughout; `n_words()` counts the
whitespace-separated words of each text.

```{r words}
n_words <- function(text) lengths(strsplit(text, "\\s+"))
with(abstracts, summary(n_words(Abstract)))
with(abstracts, sum(n_words(Abstract) > 200))
```

```{r words-numbers, include = FALSE}
abstract_words <- with(abstracts, n_words(Abstract))
```

The median abstract has `r median(abstract_words)` words and the longest
`r max(abstract_words)`. A tokenizer produces more tokens than there are
words, because rare words, numbers and punctuation are split into several
pieces, so 200 words is already close to the 256-token window.
`r format(sum(abstract_words > 200), big.mark = ",")` abstracts
(`r round(100 * mean(abstract_words > 200))`%) exceed 200 words, and the
end of each of them would be cut off if it were encoded whole.

## How finely should a document be split?

`segment()` splits each document at one of three levels. `"sentence"`
splits at `.`, `?` and `!`; `"clause"` also splits at semicolons, colons,
spaced dashes and subordinating words such as "which" and "where";
`"phrase"` also splits at commas. One invented sentence pair shows the
difference.

```{r levels-example}
example_text <- paste(
  "Engagement rose by 2.5 points (see Fig. 3, i.e. the second panel).",
  "Dr. Smith et al. argue the effect is small; others disagree, which",
  "matters for policy. Students who used the tool, especially in large",
  "classes, reported higher satisfaction."
)
segment(example_text, level = "sentence")
segment(example_text, level = "clause")
segment(example_text, level = "phrase")
```

The result has one row per segment: `document_id` (the position of the
document in the input), `document_name` (its name, empty here), `segment`
(the position within the document) and `text`. At sentence level the
example gives three segments. Neither the decimal point in "2.5", nor the
periods of "Fig.", "i.e.", "Dr." and "et al.", nor the comma inside the
parentheses ends a segment: numbers, a gazetteer of abbreviations and
parentheticals are protected. The clause level splits the second sentence
at the semicolon and before "which", and leaves the third whole, because
its commas set off an aside rather than a new clause. The phrase level
splits the third sentence at its two commas as well.

Across the corpus, the level sets the number and length of the units.
`segment_profile()` summarizes one segmentation.

```{r profile}
segment_profile <- function(segments, level) {
  with(segments, data.frame(
    level = level,
    segments = length(text),
    per_abstract = length(text) / length(unique(document_id)),
    median_words = median(n_words(text)),
    max_words = max(n_words(text))
  ))
}
sentences <- with(abstracts, segment(Abstract, level = "sentence"))
clauses <- with(abstracts, segment(Abstract, level = "clause"))
phrases <- with(abstracts, segment(Abstract, level = "phrase"))
rbind(
  segment_profile(sentences, "sentence"),
  segment_profile(clauses, "clause"),
  segment_profile(phrases, "phrase")
)
```

```{r profile-numbers, include = FALSE}
sentence_words <- with(sentences, n_words(text))
```

The sentence level turns the abstracts into
`r format(nrow(sentences), big.mark = ",")` segments, about
`r round(nrow(sentences) / nrow(abstracts))` per abstract, with a median of
`r median(sentence_words)` words. The clause level gives
`r format(nrow(clauses), big.mark = ",")` and the phrase level
`r format(nrow(phrases), big.mark = ",")`. A sentence is the natural unit
for academic prose: it usually makes one claim and is long enough to carry
meaning on its own. Phrases are often fragments ("especially in large
classes,") whose embeddings say little, so the finer levels are worth their
cost only when sentences regularly combine several ideas. The [guide to
choosing the number of topics](choosing-topics.html) compares the levels on
the quality of the resulting topics with `compare_topics()`.

## Do some segments still overrun the window?

Splitting at sentence boundaries does not bound the length of a sentence.

```{r long-sentences}
with(sentences, sum(n_words(text) > 100))
long_sentences <- subset(sentences, n_words(text) > 100)
head(long_sentences, 1)
```

`r sum(sentence_words > 100)` sentences exceed 100 words and the longest
has `r max(sentence_words)`. The first of them is a list of bullet points
joined by semicolons, which the sentence level does not split. `max_tokens`
caps the length of every segment: a segment over the budget is re-split at
the finest punctuation it contains (clause boundaries, semicolons, colons,
dashes, then commas), and the pieces are packed back up to the budget.

```{r max-tokens-example}
capped_example <- with(head(long_sentences, 1),
                       segment(text, level = "sentence", max_tokens = 40))
capped_example
```

The bulleted sentence becomes `r nrow(capped_example)` segments of
`r paste(with(capped_example, n_words(text)), collapse = ", ")` words: the
first ends at a semicolon, the second at a comma, and the third at the end
of the sentence. Without
a model, `max_tokens` counts words, a deterministic offline proxy; because a
tokenizer emits more tokens than words, the budget is set below the model's
window, for example 200 words for a 256-token model, or 100 words for the
128-token multilingual models. With a loaded model, `segment(..., model =
model)` counts that model's exact tokens instead, and `max_tokens` can be
the window itself.

```{r max-tokens-corpus}
capped <- with(abstracts, segment(Abstract, level = "sentence", max_tokens = 100))
segment_profile(capped, "sentence, max_tokens = 100")
```

```{r max-tokens-corpus-numbers, include = FALSE}
capped_words <- with(capped, n_words(text))
```

With a budget of 100 words, the corpus has
`r format(nrow(capped), big.mark = ",")` sentence segments instead of
`r format(nrow(sentences), big.mark = ",")`, and none is longer than
`r max(capped_words)` words. Only the over-long sentences change.

`topics()`, `topic_corpus()` and `compare_topics()` take the same
`max_tokens`, `merge_below` and `min_content` options as `segment()`, so the
segmentation used to encode and the one used to fit can be made to agree.

## Which abbreviations end a sentence?

A period after an abbreviation is the most common cause of a wrong
sentence split. `abbreviations()` returns the built-in gazetteer.

```{r gazetteer}
abbreviations()
```

The gazetteer holds `r length(abbreviations())` abbreviations common in
academic writing. Matching ignores case and starts at a word boundary, so
"St." in "St. Petersburg" is protected but the end of "cost." is not. An
abbreviation that is missing splits a sentence in the wrong place:

```{r custom-abbreviation}
segment("Results are reported in Sect. 4. The model fits well.",
        level = "sentence")
segment("Results are reported in Sect. 4. The model fits well.",
        level = "sentence", abbreviations = c(abbreviations(), "SECT."))
```

With the default gazetteer, "Sect." ends a sentence and "4." becomes a
segment of its own. Adding `"SECT."` to the gazetteer gives the two correct
sentences. A domain with its own abbreviations (law, medicine, a
non-English source) needs its own additions.

## How are fragments and reference noise handled?

Abstracts and full texts contain material that is not prose: copyright
lines, citations, page ranges and numbered lists. At clause level these
become segments of their own.

```{r noise}
noisy <- paste(
  "Teachers adapted quickly to remote teaching. (2020), 12(3), 45-67.",
  "doi:10.1000/xyz 2021; 14: 1-9. Most reported fatigue."
)
noisy_segments <- segment(noisy, level = "clause")
noisy_segments
with(noisy_segments, content_ratio(text))
```

`content_ratio()` is the share of a segment's characters that belong to
alphabetic words. The two sentences of prose score above 0.9; the citation
fragments score 0.3 or less. `min_content` drops every segment below a
floor.

```{r min-content}
segment(noisy, level = "clause", min_content = 0.5)
```

A floor of 0.5 keeps the two prose sentences and removes the four
fragments. On the abstracts:

```{r min-content-corpus}
with(clauses, sum(content_ratio(text) < 0.5))
head(subset(clauses, content_ratio(text) < 0.5), 4)
```

```{r min-content-numbers, include = FALSE}
low_content <- with(clauses, sum(content_ratio(text) < 0.5))
```

`r format(low_content, big.mark = ",")` of the
`r format(nrow(clauses), big.mark = ",")` clauses fall below 0.5, among
them copyright lines that publishers append to abstracts. Left in, such
fragments tend to gather into a topic of their own that describes the
publisher, not the research.

`merge_below` handles short fragments that are prose: a segment with fewer
words than the threshold is joined to its neighbor.

```{r merge-below}
segment(example_text, level = "phrase", merge_below = 4)
with(clauses, sum(n_words(text) < 4))
merged <- with(abstracts, segment(Abstract, level = "clause", merge_below = 4))
nrow(merged)
```

With `merge_below = 4`, "others disagree," (two words) is joined to the
segment before it, and "reported higher satisfaction." (three words) to the
one before that. In the abstracts,
`r format(with(clauses, sum(n_words(text) < 4)), big.mark = ",")` clauses
have fewer than four words, and merging reduces the clause count from
`r format(nrow(clauses), big.mark = ",")` to
`r format(nrow(merged), big.mark = ",")`. Merging changes the units the
model is fitted to, so it is a choice to state and keep fixed, like the
level.

## How does a topic model use segments?

`topics()` takes the same options through `segment`, `max_tokens`,
`merge_below` and `min_content`: it segments every document, embeds every
segment, and clusters the segments. The example below is a toy: four short
course reviews of two sentences each, with three-dimensional embeddings
written by hand so that the result can be followed. The first dimension
stands for teaching quality, the second for workload and assessment.

```{r toy-data}
reviews <- c(
  course_a = "The lectures were clear. Overall it was fine.",
  course_b = "The exam was far too long. Overall it was fine.",
  course_c = "The teacher explained every step. The slides helped.",
  course_d = "The workload was heavy. Grading felt unfair."
)
review_sentences <- segment(reviews, level = "sentence")
review_sentences
```

The four reviews give eight sentences. The toy embeddings have one row per
sentence, in the order `segment()` returns them. The sentence "Overall it
was fine." appears in two reviews and gets the same, ambiguous vector both
times, as it would from a real encoder, which sees only the sentence.

```{r toy-fit}
sentence_embeddings <- rbind(
  c(0.95, 0.05, 0.10), c(0.50, 0.50, 0.40),
  c(0.05, 0.95, 0.10), c(0.50, 0.50, 0.40),
  c(0.90, 0.10, 0.15), c(0.85, 0.15, 0.10),
  c(0.10, 0.90, 0.15), c(0.15, 0.85, 0.10)
)
sentence_model <- topics(reviews, n_topics = 2, segment = "sentence",
                         embeddings = sentence_embeddings, n_terms = 3)
sentence_model
as.data.frame(sentence_model, what = "documents")
```

The model has one row per segment, not per document: the document table
carries `document_id`, `document_name` and `segment` next to each
sentence's topic. The teaching sentences form one topic and the workload
sentences the other; both copies of "Overall it was fine." join the
teaching topic, including the one in `course_b`, a review about the exam.

Segment-level and document-level counts answer different questions.

```{r toy-sizes}
topic_sizes(sentence_model)
topic_sizes(sentence_model, by = "document")
```

By segment, the teaching topic holds 5 of the 8 sentences. By document, a
review counts once for every topic it reaches, so the proportions are
shares of the 4 reviews and add to more than one: the teaching topic
reaches 3 reviews and the workload topic 2. `topic_gamma()` gives each
review's mixture, the share of its segments in each topic.

```{r toy-gamma}
topic_gamma(sentence_model)
topic_gamma(sentence_model, top = 1)
```

`course_b` is split half and half; the other three reviews fall wholly in
one topic. `top = 1` keeps each document's dominant topic, with the first
topic winning a tie. No encoding happens here: a segmented model stores the
topic of every segment, so its mixtures are counts.

## Can a segment borrow context from its document?

The ambiguous sentence shows the price of segmenting: a short segment can
be ambiguous on its own, and identical segments in different documents get
identical vectors. `blend()` mixes each segment's vector with that of its
parent document. It keeps `alpha` of what the segment says beyond its
document (the part of the segment vector orthogonal to the document vector)
and `1 - alpha` of the document direction, and normalizes the result to
unit length. The toy document embeddings below point toward teaching for
`course_a` and `course_c` and toward workload for `course_b` and
`course_d`.

```{r toy-blend}
document_embeddings <- rbind(
  c(0.85, 0.30, 0.20), c(0.30, 0.85, 0.20),
  c(0.95, 0.10, 0.10), c(0.10, 0.95, 0.10)
)
contextual <- blend(review_sentences, alpha = 0.5,
                    embeddings = sentence_embeddings,
                    document_embeddings = document_embeddings)
round(contextual, 3)
```

The two copies of "Overall it was fine." (rows 2 and 4) now differ: the one
in `course_a` leans toward the first dimension, the one in `course_b` toward
the second. Fitting the topics to the blended vectors:

```{r toy-blend-fit}
blended_model <- topics(reviews, n_topics = 2, segment = "sentence",
                        embeddings = contextual, n_terms = 3)
topic_gamma(blended_model)
```

Each copy of the ambiguous sentence now joins the topic of its own review,
and every review falls wholly in one topic. `alpha = 0` would replace every
segment with its document, and `alpha = 1` would keep only what the segment
adds to its document; the default 0.5 balances the two. Blending suits
corpora in which short segments are common and their meaning depends on
the document. The blended matrix must be built from the same segmentation
that `topics()` applies, which here means the same `level` and the same
segmentation options.

## The same analysis on the abstracts

With a downloaded model, the analysis above runs on the abstracts. The code
is not run here because it needs the model (see the [guide to models and
the cache](models-and-cache.html)).

```{r covid-fit, eval = FALSE}
model <- load_model("all-MiniLM-L6-v2")
sentence_model <- topics(abstracts, column = "Abstract", n_topics = 8,
                         segment = "sentence", max_tokens = 256,
                         min_content = 0.5, model = model)
summary(sentence_model)
topic_sizes(sentence_model, by = "document")
topic_gamma(sentence_model, top = 3)
```

With a model and `max_tokens`, `topics()` counts the model's own tokens, so
the budget can be the 256-token window. To blend, the segments are taken
from `segment()` with a word budget, because `blend()` and `topics()` must
see the same segmentation and precomputed embeddings make `topics()` count
words:

```{r covid-blend, eval = FALSE}
covid_sentences <- with(abstracts, segment(Abstract, level = "sentence",
                                           max_tokens = 200))
contextual <- with(abstracts, blend(covid_sentences, documents = Abstract,
                                    model = model, alpha = 0.5))
blended_model <- topics(abstracts, column = "Abstract", n_topics = 8,
                        segment = "sentence", max_tokens = 200,
                        embeddings = contextual)
topic_gamma(blended_model, top = 3)
```

## When to segment, and how

- Documents that fit the model's window and make one point (feedback
  messages, short answers, titles): no segmentation; see [the main
  article](sbert.html).
- Documents longer than the window, or documents that discuss several
  themes: `segment = "sentence"`, with `max_tokens` set to the window (with
  a model) or somewhat below it in words.
- Text with citations, copyright lines or lists: add `min_content = 0.5`,
  or clean the documents first (see [preparing a
  corpus](preparing-corpus.html)).
- Short, context-dependent segments: `blend()` the segment and document
  vectors before fitting.
- Unsure which level: compare them with `compare_topics(segment = c(...))`
  (see [choosing the number of topics](choosing-topics.html)); mixtures of
  new documents are covered in [assigning topics](assigning-topics.html).

```{r reset, include = FALSE}
options(old_options)
```
